clue.text: Perhaps one of the characters in Guys and Dolls, hoping to be better (Teddy was one).

definitions.text: Perhaps one of the characters in Guys and Dolls, hoping to be better
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read in pieces: a BIG gambler out HUNTing a GAME, like the high rollers of the musical Guys and Dolls, each hoping to win as a bettor
second meaning: Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt was famous for shooting lions and elephants on safari

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is a pun on 'bettor', one who bets; the gamblers of Guys and Dolls hunt for a big game of craps. Teddy Roosevelt's African safaris made him the most famous shooter of large animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who hunts large wild animals such as lions for sport; Roosevelt led a celebrated African safari after his presidency.

clue.text: What I do when I flash a big smile in support?

definitions.text: What I do when I flash a big smile
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: when I smile broadly
second meaning: a steel girder with an I-shaped cross-section, used to hold up a structure

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as 'I' plus 'beam', to smile radiantly, for the first reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A steel girder shaped like a capital I in section is a standard structural member that bears loads in buildings.

clue.text: What a professional rider has to do to progress?

definitions.text: What a professional rider has to do
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: a jockey must climb on the horse he is paid to ride
second meaning: to carry on making headway with a task

explanation.walkthrough: The jockey literally mounts the animal that is his work; the idiom means pressing ahead with a task.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means continuing a piece of work without delay, which is making headway with it.

clue.text: A southern neighbor has me with a number of football players, and a little company to provide it.

parts.note: taken as written
a soccer team has eleven players, written XI in Roman numerals
CO is the short form of company

explanation.surface: A neighbouring country to the south seems to be lending a sports team and a small firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' and 'and ... to provide it' only string the pieces together; the eleven-a-side team gives the Roman numeral XI.
explanation.definitionFit: The country borders the United States along its southern frontier, so it is the American setter's southern neighbor.

clue.text: Drunk, as they say, but there's no getting on with it in the classic movie.

parts.note: high is slang for intoxicated, as they say
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is too intoxicated to cope with an old film classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As they say' flags high as a colloquial word for drunk; 'getting ... with it' merely joins NO to ON.
explanation.definitionFit: High Noon (1952), starring Gary Cooper as a lone marshal, is one of the best-known Westerns ever filmed.

clue.text: What isolationists preached might be not in! Not in? Never!

indicators.note: these words could be rearranged into something else, so the letters that follow are shuffled

explanation.surface: Isolationists shout their slogan: never get involved, never be in!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might be' asks what the letters of NOTIN, NOTIN and NEVER could become when rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolationists argued that a nation should keep out of other countries' wars and affairs, a policy of staying uninvolved.

clue.text: In part when I sleep, I cure another person of sensitive taste.

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used, so the answer lies concealed inside them

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of sleep through I cure into the start of another

explanation.surface: A cure taken while asleep turns someone into a refined gourmet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In part' says only part of the words is used: the answer runs from the end of 'sleep' through 'I cure' into the start of 'another'.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of refined pleasures, especially good food and drink, is someone with discriminating taste.

clue.text: One of the Yellow Pages might be an expensive put-on!

parts.note: gold is a yellow colour
a leaf is a page of a book

explanation.surface: An entry in the Yellow Pages phone directory proves a costly sham.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yellow Pages is a printed business telephone directory. 'Put-on' looks like a hoax but is something applied to a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold beaten into very thin sheets is applied to frames and lettering, a costly gilded coating.

clue.text: Iron? Bronze? They're examples of what one does in time.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Iron Age and the Bronze Age are prehistoric periods
second meaning: as a verb, a person grows older over time

explanation.walkthrough: The metals stand for the prehistoric periods named after them, plural noun; the second reading is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaeological periods are named after the material in use, and as a verb the word means growing older.

clue.text: An obvious tool for the woodsman, but that's what the country does, according to some people!

definitions.text: what the country does, according to some people

parts.note: overt means open and plain to see
an ax (American spelling of axe) is the woodcutter's tool

explanation.surface: A woodcutter's plain axe is compared to how the state treats its citizens.
explanation.walkthrough: AX is the American spelling, natural in this US magazine puzzle. 'According to some people' fairly hedges the political opinion that the government taxes too much.
explanation.definitionFit: To levy excessive charges on citizens is what critics say the government does with its revenue demands.

clue.text: Drink and make merry with music — the oriental says it's good for you!

parts.note: gin is a spirit, a drink
to sing is to make merry with music

explanation.surface: Have a gin and a singsong, and an Eastern sage assures you it is healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The oriental says' tells you the herb's Eastern name is entered as it sounds, GIN-SING; the hidden word at 7 Down confirms the I. The usual English spelling has an E in that place.
explanation.definitionFit: The root of this Asian plant is taken as a tonic and is traditionally believed to boost health and energy.

clue.text: Act put on with a short skirt, getting able to see the Republic, possibly.

parts.note: to do is to act or perform
a mini is a skirt ending well above the knee
can means to be able to

explanation.surface: A performer in a miniskirt is hoping to travel to see a republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on with', 'getting' and 'to see' only link the pieces; 'possibly' marks the Republic as one example of what the answer can describe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dominican Republic shares the Caribbean island of Hispaniola with Haiti, so the adjective names that nation.

clue.text: They may be proper, or quite common — implying an absence of sunburst.

definitions.text: They may be proper, or quite common

parts.note: an absence of something is no amount of it, giving NO

indicators.note: something burst is broken apart, so the letters of sun are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Things might be respectable or vulgar, suggesting there was no sudden sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proper' and 'common' look like social class but are grammar terms. 'Sunburst' must be split: 'burst' scrambles sun into UNS, which follows NO.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar divides naming words into proper ones (capitalised names like Paris) and common ones (like city).

clue.text: Even a bad priest might show such sprightly wit.

indicators.note: a bad version is a corrupted one, so the word's letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Even a poor clergyman can display some lively humour.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loan word means liveliness of mind and quick cleverness in conversation.

clue.text: Left on top, the rest comes up with a greasy liquid of this in case it's for the papers.

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece placed on top of the rest comes first

parts.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship

indicators.note: in a down answer, coming up means being read from bottom to top, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: oil is a greasy liquid
taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzling sequence about oil leaking out, ending with a case of documents.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'on top' means placed first, and 'comes up' reads OIL OF upwards as FOLIO. Port is the sailor's word for left.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat carrying case holds loose documents, drawings or papers, keeping them flat and together.

clue.text: The kind of supper a dog enjoys might be responsible for much growth.

definitions.text: The kind of supper a dog enjoys
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read in pieces: a dinner of bones

definitions.text: might be responsible for much growth
definitions.meaning: second meaning: ground animal bones used as garden fertilizer

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, a meal of bones, for the dog; as one thing it is a fertilizer.
explanation.definitionFit: Crushed animal bones are spread on soil as a slow-release fertilizer that feeds plants.

clue.text: Continue to prevaricate? Be quiet!

definitions.meaning: second meaning: stay motionless and silent

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading uses 'still' to mean 'even now' and 'lie' as telling falsehoods; the second is keeping motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: To remain motionless and calm without fidgeting is to keep quiet in the physical sense.

clue.text: Once containing a sour mixture, it certainly wasn't off the beam!

definitions.text: it certainly wasn't off the beam

indicators.note: Once holding the following letters within it, so they are placed inside that word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a mixture blends things, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A former sour cocktail is compared to something on target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixture' jumbles sour into OURS and 'containing' places it inside once. Off the beam is old aviation slang for straying from the radio beam that guided pilots.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane flying along a radio beam is on track; heading in the right direction means not having strayed.

clue.text: A little bit of money, as the British once said, should be quite a distant object.

definitions.text: A little bit of money, as the British once said
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old British coin worth a quarter of a penny

definitions.text: should be quite a distant object
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: A farthing was an old British coin, a quarter of a penny, withdrawn in 1960. Split the answer as 'far thing' for the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The coin was the smallest British denomination, a quarter of an old penny, hence a tiny sum.

clue.text: See 22
Mar the surface between C and G, with one in the card game.

parts.note: the letters lying between C and G in the alphabet are D, E and F
an ace counts as one in card games

explanation.surface: Someone scratches a table while dealing cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' only joins the pieces; the alphabet run from C to G gives the letters in between.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil the appearance of something by marking or disfiguring it is to damage its outward look.

clue.text: If fit enuf, have a fling with one of the main drags!

indicators.note: a fling throws things about, so the letters of these words are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: If you are fit enough, go dancing on a major street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A fling with' tosses the letters of FIT ENUF and HAVE into a new order; the joke misspelling 'enuf' supplies exactly the letters needed, and 'If' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Fifth Avenue is a principal thoroughfare of Manhattan, and a main drag is American slang for a town's chief street.

clue.text: Little 17 without the register?

parts.note: 17 is LIE STILL; take away TILL, a cash register, and LIES remain; little ones are small untruths

explanation.walkthrough: Removing a till, a shop's cash register, from 17's answer leaves the plural untruths; 'Little' makes them minor ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Small trivial untruths told to avoid trouble are minor lies, exactly what 'little' qualifies here.

clue.text: The roving, roving traveler might have such a case!

definitions.text: The roving, roving traveler might have such a case!

parts.words: The roving, roving traveler might have such a case
parts.note: a traveller always on the move needs a small bag holding just enough for one night away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' seems legal or medical but is luggage: a small suitcase for a short stay.
explanation.definitionFit: A small suitcase holding enough clothes and toiletries for a single night's stay is named for that short trip.

clue.text: The arrangement of fiber in wood or cereal?

definitions.text: The arrangement of fiber in wood
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the pattern of fibres running through timber
second meaning: seed of crops such as wheat or barley

explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both the visible fibre pattern of timber and harvested wheat or barley.
explanation.definitionFit: The direction of fibres in timber is its pattern, and wheat and barley harvests are collectively seed crops.

clue.text: A ringer with a short, sharp shock — holding an experiment in the lab, perhaps.

definitions.text: holding an experiment in the lab, perhaps

parts.note: a bell is something that rings
a jar is a sudden jolt

explanation.surface: A bell rings with a jolt as someone carries out a laboratory test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the two pieces; 'perhaps' admits the vessel has other uses.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass dome placed over apparatus or specimens in a laboratory keeps them sealed or under vacuum.

clue.text: A rather large trouble for the maid, as they used to say!

definitions.text: the maid, as they used to say

parts.note: big means large
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A housemaid has quite a big problem, in old-fashioned language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' only links the pieces. 'As they used to say' signals the dated usage: an abigail was a lady's maid, after a character in a 17th-century play.
explanation.definitionFit: Abigail was once a generic name for a lady's personal servant, from a character in Beaumont and Fletcher's play.

clue.text: The stuntman for the actor has a purpose, but you might be expected to get it with a pun.

definitions.text: you might be expected to get it with a pun

parts.note: a double stands in for an actor in risky scenes
meaning is the purpose or intent behind something

explanation.surface: An actor's stand-in has an aim, but a joke might give you the idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' and 'but' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun works by exploiting a word that can be read in two senses at once, giving a second sense.
